cases.title: Leg Pain on Walking
cases.initial: A 54-year-old man reports gradually worsening pain in both legs over the past year. He has begun cutting back on walks and errands.

questions: Walking or standing for several minutes brings on aching and heaviness in his legs.
Sitting usually relieves symptoms within a few minutes. Simply stopping while standing helps much less.
Yes. Leaning over a shopping cart lets him walk much farther.
It involves both buttocks and the back of the thighs, sometimes extending into the calves.
Does walking uphill or downhill differ?
Downhill walking is more difficult than uphill walking.
He tolerates a stationary bicycle much better than upright walking.
He has hypertension and previously smoked; he has no known peripheral arterial disease.
Any new bladder, saddle, or progressive weakness symptoms?
No bowel or bladder changes, saddle sensory changes, or progressive focal weakness.
Both feet are warm, and distal pulses are palpable bilaterally.
What is the neurological examination at rest?
Lower-extremity strength, reflexes, and light-touch sensation are broadly normal at rest.
What does straight leg raise show?
Straight leg raise does not reproduce his characteristic symptoms.
Extension is restricted and increases discomfort; flexion is better tolerated.
cases.debrief: The patient's bilateral leg discomfort is brought on by standing or walking and relieved by sitting or lumbar flexion. His improvement when leaning forward, along with greater difficulty walking downhill than uphill, makes neurogenic claudication particularly likely. This remains a clinical working diagnosis, as lumbar imaging has not yet confirmed stenosis.
key_points: Flexion-related relief and the shopping-cart pattern help distinguish neurogenic from vascular claudication.
Normal resting neurological findings do not exclude lumbar spinal stenosis.
Assess vascular risk and red flags rather than relying on one characteristic clue.
cases.caution: A clinical working diagnosis; imaging is considered in context, especially if symptoms are persistent or intervention is contemplated.
imaging: Any previous lumbar MRI or CT?
He has not had a lumbar MRI or CT.

alternatives.name: Peripheral arterial disease
alternatives.distinction: Exertional leg discomfort and his vascular risk factors make peripheral arterial disease an important alternative. Vascular claudication typically improves with rest even without sitting or bending forward, whereas this patient's symptoms are strongly influenced by posture. Palpable pulses do not exclude arterial disease.

alternatives.name: Lumbar radicular pain
alternatives.distinction: Radicular pain can radiate into the legs, but it more often follows a recognizable nerve root distribution and may be accompanied by neurological deficits or positive neural tension testing. These findings are not prominent in this presentation.

alternatives.name: Peripheral neuropathy
alternatives.distinction: Peripheral neuropathy is another possible cause of leg discomfort, particularly when sensory symptoms are present. However, symptoms are generally more persistent and distally distributed rather than consistently provoked by standing and relieved by spinal flexion.

findings.title: Symptoms provoked by standing or walking
findings.reviewed: Neurogenic and vascular claudication can both produce exertional leg symptoms. The relationship with prolonged standing provides an additional clue toward a spinal mechanism.
findings.unreviewed: Asking whether standing as well as walking provokes symptoms could help distinguish a spinal mechanism from exertional leg pain alone.

findings.title: Relief with sitting rather than standing rest
findings.reviewed: Relief with sitting is especially informative because it suggests that changing spinal posture matters, rather than simply stopping physical activity.
findings.unreviewed: Comparing relief from sitting with relief from simply stopping while standing could help establish whether spinal posture influences the symptoms.

findings.title: Improvement with lumbar flexion
findings.reviewed: The shopping cart sign supports neurogenic claudication because lumbar flexion can increase the available space around neural structures and reduce symptom provocation.
findings.unreviewed: Asking whether leaning forward improves walking tolerance could help establish whether lumbar flexion relieves the symptoms.

supporting_findings.title: Walking slope
supporting_findings.reviewed: Greater difficulty walking downhill than uphill adds support for a spinal mechanism because downhill walking tends to involve more lumbar extension.

supporting_findings.title: Cycling tolerance
supporting_findings.reviewed: Better tolerance of cycling than upright walking adds support for a posture dependent pattern rather than exertion alone.

supporting_findings.title: Lumbar movement
supporting_findings.reviewed: Discomfort with extension and better tolerance of flexion reinforce the relationship between symptoms and spinal posture.

next_steps.title: Complete the assessment
next_steps.text: Clarify the effect on walking tolerance and daily function, complete the neurological and vascular examinations, and screen for new neurological red flags.

next_steps.title: Investigations
next_steps.text: Consider lumbar MRI when symptoms remain functionally limiting or when imaging would guide further management, particularly before an intervention. If peripheral arterial disease remains a concern, obtain an ankle brachial index.

next_steps.title: Management
next_steps.text: Discuss individualized conservative management, including physiotherapy, exercise, and strategies to maintain activity. Persistent functional limitations may warrant specialist assessment. New bowel or bladder dysfunction, saddle sensory changes, or progressive neurological weakness require urgent evaluation.

cases.title: Back and Leg Pain
cases.initial: A 38-year-old woman reports three weeks of lower back and left leg pain. Sitting through her workday has become increasingly uncomfortable.
cases.debrief: The combination of radiating leg pain, tingling over the dorsal foot, a positive straight leg raise, and mild great toe extension weakness supports involvement of the left L5 nerve root. A disc herniation is one possible cause, but no imaging has established the underlying structural lesion.
questions: The pain travels from her lower back through the left buttock and outer calf toward the top of her foot.
What does the pain feel like?
She describes a sharp, electric pain with occasional tingling.
Prolonged sitting, bending forward, and coughing can aggravate the radiating pain.
Changing position and brief periods of walking usually help. She is not limited by a predictable walking distance.
She occasionally notices tingling over the top of her left foot and toward the great toe.
She occasionally catches her left toe on stairs, but has not fallen. She has not noticed rapidly worsening weakness.
Symptoms began after a weekend of moving furniture. There was no fall or major injury.
She reports no new bowel or bladder dysfunction, saddle sensory changes, or progressive weakness.
Left straight leg raise reproduces her characteristic radiating pain at approximately 40 degrees. The right side is negative.
Left great toe extension is mildly weak at 4+/5. Ankle dorsiflexion is nearly full, and plantarflexion is preserved.
Light touch is slightly reduced over the left dorsal foot near the great toe. Patellar and Achilles reflexes are symmetric.
Hip movement is painless. Heel walking is mildly more difficult on the left, without a pronounced foot drop.
imaging: No prior lumbar MRI or CT is available for this presentation.

display_labels.h02: What does the pain feel like?

alternatives.name: Common fibular neuropathy
alternatives.distinction: A fibular nerve lesion can cause dorsal foot sensory symptoms and weakness of toe extension or ankle dorsiflexion. However, pain beginning in the lower back, radiating down the leg, and reproduced by straight leg raise favours a nerve root process.

alternatives.name: Nonspecific mechanical low back pain
alternatives.distinction: Mechanical back pain can be aggravated by movement and prolonged sitting. It is less likely to explain a consistent radiating leg pattern with sensory changes and focal weakness.

findings.title: Pain distribution
findings.reviewed: Radiation from the lower back through the outer leg toward the dorsal foot helps localize symptoms to a lumbar nerve root, particularly L5.
findings.unreviewed: Clarifying the complete distribution of pain would help distinguish a lumbar nerve root pattern from a peripheral nerve or local musculoskeletal problem.

findings.title: Straight leg raise
findings.reviewed: Reproduction of her characteristic radiating pain during straight leg raise supports irritation of a lumbosacral nerve root. The test should be interpreted alongside the history and neurological examination.
findings.unreviewed: Straight leg raise could help determine whether neural tension reproduces the patient's characteristic radiating symptoms.

findings.title: Great toe extension weakness
findings.reviewed: Mild weakness of great toe extension provides an objective neurological finding compatible with L5 involvement.
findings.unreviewed: Testing great toe extension and ankle strength could identify objective weakness and improve anatomical localization.

next_steps.title: Assessment and initial care
next_steps.text: Document neurological function, monitor for progression, and discuss maintaining tolerable activity and appropriate conservative treatment, including physiotherapy and symptom management.

next_steps.title: When to investigate further
next_steps.text: Consider lumbar MRI if symptoms persist despite appropriate management, if an intervention is being considered, or if a significant neurological deficit develops. Progressive motor weakness or new cauda equina symptoms require urgent assessment.

cases.title: Persistent Shoulder Pain
cases.initial: A 51-year-old teacher reports three months of right shoulder pain. Reaching and lifting have become uncomfortable, although she cannot recall a specific injury.
cases.debrief: The combination of lateral shoulder pain, symptoms with overhead activity, painful resisted rotator cuff testing, and relatively preserved passive movement supports a rotator cuff related pain disorder. The largely preserved strength and absence of a significant traumatic event make a major acute cuff tear less likely.
questions: Reaching overhead and lifting objects away from her body are particularly uncomfortable.
She sometimes wakes when lying on her right shoulder.
She describes discomfort at the end of some movements but does not feel that the joint is globally stiff.
There was no fall, sudden injury, or abrupt loss of shoulder strength.
She has no significant neck pain, radiating arm symptoms, or hand tingling.
The pain is mainly over the lateral shoulder and sometimes extends partway down the upper arm.
She reports no fever, unexplained weight loss, or other constitutional symptoms.
Dressing remains possible, but overhead household tasks and gardening have become more difficult.
Active abduction is painful through the middle of its range. Passive shoulder movement is nearly full and considerably less painful.
Resisted abduction and external rotation reproduce lateral shoulder pain, but strength is largely preserved.
Signs of a major cuff tear?
Drop arm and external rotation lag tests are negative. There is no pronounced objective weakness.
Cervical movement is comfortable, Spurling testing is negative, and the upper limb neurological examination is normal.
imaging: Radiographs show preserved glenohumeral joint space with mild acromioclavicular degenerative changes. There is no acute bony abnormality. No ultrasound or MRI has been performed.

display_labels.e03: Signs of a major cuff tear?

alternatives.name: Adhesive capsulitis
alternatives.distinction: Adhesive capsulitis produces progressive restriction of both active and passive movement, particularly external rotation. This patient's passive movement is largely preserved.

alternatives.name: Glenohumeral osteoarthritis
alternatives.distinction: Osteoarthritis may cause shoulder pain and stiffness, but generally produces greater passive movement restriction and degenerative changes on radiographs.

alternatives.name: Full thickness rotator cuff tear
alternatives.distinction: A substantial tear can produce weakness and difficulty elevating the arm. Her preserved strength and negative lag testing make a large tear less likely, although examination alone cannot exclude every tear.

findings.title: Active and passive movement
findings.reviewed: Painful active movement with preserved passive range helps distinguish rotator cuff related pain from conditions that restrict the glenohumeral joint itself.
findings.unreviewed: Comparing active and passive movement could help determine whether pain or joint restriction is the principal limitation.

findings.title: Resisted rotator cuff testing
findings.reviewed: Pain reproduced by resisted abduction and external rotation supports a rotator cuff related source. No single provocative test is independently diagnostic.
findings.unreviewed: Resisted shoulder testing could help identify pain associated with rotator cuff loading.

supporting_findings.title: Preserved strength and negative lag testing
supporting_findings.reviewed: Largely preserved strength and negative drop arm and external rotation lag tests make a major cuff tear less likely, although examination cannot exclude every tear.

next_steps.title: Initial management
next_steps.text: Discuss activity modification that preserves function, patient education, and progressive exercise based rehabilitation focusing on shoulder mobility and rotator cuff loading.

next_steps.title: Follow-up
next_steps.text: Reassess pain, strength, and function after an appropriate period of treatment. Ultrasound or further specialist assessment may be useful if symptoms persist, significant weakness emerges, or a structural tear becomes more likely.

cases.title: Hand Tingling
cases.initial: A 44-year-old graphic designer reports several months of intermittent tingling in her right hand. Her work involves long periods of drawing with a stylus.
aliases: right median neuropathy at the wrist
median nerve compression at the carpal tunnel
median nerve entrapment at the wrist
compression of the median nerve at the wrist
median nerve compression at the wrist
right median nerve compression at the wrist
median nerve entrapment in the carpal tunnel
right median nerve entrapment at the wrist
median neuropathy at the wrist (carpal tunnel syndrome)
questions: Tingling is most noticeable in the thumb, index, and middle fingers, sometimes reaching the thumb side of the ring finger.
It frequently wakes her at night and sometimes appears while holding her phone or driving.
Shaking out the hand or changing wrist position usually eases the tingling within a few minutes.
Any symptoms in the little finger?
The little finger is generally spared.
Any neck or radiating arm pain?
She has no neck pain or shooting discomfort travelling from the neck down the arm.
She occasionally struggles to grip a pen when the hand feels numb, but has not noticed sustained weakness.
Any symptoms in the other hand?
She has mild occasional tingling in the left fingertips, but the right hand is much more troublesome.
Any relevant health or work history?
She spends hours drawing with a stylus. She has no known diabetes or thyroid disorder.
Light touch feels mildly reduced over the right index and middle fingertips. Sensation over the little finger is preserved.
Sustained compression over the volar carpal tunnel reproduces her familiar tingling in the thumb and first two fingers.
Thenar muscle bulk is preserved. Thumb palmar abduction is full, with no clear objective weakness.
Cervical movement does not reproduce symptoms. There is no consistent ulnar sensory loss or intrinsic hand weakness.

cases.debrief: The nocturnal tingling, median nerve sensory distribution, little finger sparing, and reproduction of symptoms with carpal tunnel compression favour median nerve entrapment at the wrist. Preserved thenar bulk and thumb strength suggest that marked motor involvement is not apparent on this examination.

alternatives.name: Cervical radiculopathy
alternatives.distinction: Cervical nerve root irritation can produce hand paresthesia, but it more often involves associated neck or radiating arm symptoms and does not necessarily follow an isolated median nerve territory.

alternatives.name: Ulnar neuropathy
alternatives.distinction: This commonly affects the little finger and ulnar side of the ring finger, making it less consistent with her symptom distribution.

alternatives.name: Peripheral neuropathy
alternatives.distinction: A generalized neuropathy more commonly causes persistent, often bilateral distal sensory symptoms and may involve the feet. Her clearly positional, nocturnal hand symptoms are more focal.

findings.title: Median distribution
findings.reviewed: Tingling in the thumb, index, and middle fingers suggests median sensory involvement, though symptom distributions can overlap.
findings.unreviewed: Asking exactly which fingers are affected would help distinguish median nerve entrapment from an ulnar or cervical source.

findings.title: Nocturnal symptoms
findings.reviewed: Hand paresthesia that wakes the patient at night is a characteristic feature of carpal tunnel syndrome.
findings.unreviewed: Clarifying the timing of symptoms could reveal a typical nocturnal pattern.

findings.title: Carpal tunnel compression
findings.reviewed: Reproduction of the familiar tingling by local wrist compression supports carpal tunnel syndrome. The maneuver is supportive, not diagnostic on its own.
findings.unreviewed: Focused wrist compression could add supporting evidence, although no single provocative maneuver confirms the diagnosis.

supporting_findings.title: Little finger sparing
supporting_findings.reviewed: Preserved sensation in the little finger further supports a median rather than ulnar distribution.

next_steps.title: Initial treatment
next_steps.text: Discuss neutral position night wrist splinting, symptom provoking activities, and a plan to reassess sensory symptoms, sleep, strength, and hand function.

next_steps.title: Escalation
next_steps.text: Consider electrodiagnostic testing if the diagnosis is uncertain, symptoms are atypical, or surgery is being considered. Persistent disabling symptoms, thenar weakness, or muscle wasting merit timely hand surgery or specialist assessment.

cases.title: New Foot Weakness
cases.initial: A 46-year-old man has noticed his right foot slapping against the ground over the past three weeks. He also reports intermittent lower back discomfort and is concerned that the symptoms may be related.
cases.intended: Right common fibular neuropathy at the fibular head
cases.debrief: Weakness of dorsiflexion, toe extension, and eversion with preserved inversion supports a lesion of the common fibular nerve. The sensory changes over the dorsal foot and lateral shin, together with local nerve provocation, further support this localization. The left sided lumbar MRI finding does not explain the right sided deficits.
questions: He gradually noticed difficulty lifting the front of his right foot over several days.
He occasionally experiences mild lower back discomfort, but has no current shooting pain from the back into the leg.
He describes tingling over the outer right shin and top of the foot.
He has recently spent long periods sitting with his legs crossed while working at a desk.
He has intentionally lost approximately seven kilograms over the past three months.
There has been no recent knee injury, surgery, cast, or major trauma.
His toes sometimes catch the floor, particularly when walking quickly. He has not noticed weakness elsewhere.
He reports no facial or arm weakness, speech changes, bowel or bladder changes, or progressive bilateral symptoms.
Right ankle dorsiflexion and toe extension are weak at approximately 3/5. Ankle eversion is also weak.
Right ankle inversion, plantarflexion, and hip abduction are preserved at 5/5.
Sensation is reduced over the lateral shin and dorsal foot, including the first web space. Plantar foot sensation is preserved.
Lower limb reflexes are symmetric. Straight leg raise is negative, and tapping near the fibular neck reproduces tingling over the dorsal foot.
imaging: A recently obtained lumbar MRI shows mild degenerative changes, including a small left L4–L5 disc protrusion. There is no convincing right sided nerve root compression. No electrodiagnostic studies or dedicated fibular nerve imaging have yet been performed.

alternatives.name: L5 radiculopathy
alternatives.distinction: L5 involvement can cause weakness of dorsiflexion and toe extension. However, weakness may also involve inversion or hip abduction because these movements depend on L5 muscles supplied by nerves other than the common fibular nerve. Preserved inversion and hip abduction favour a more distal lesion in this case.

alternatives.name: Sciatic neuropathy
alternatives.distinction: Sciatic nerve injury can affect the fibular division and cause foot drop. Broader weakness or sensory changes involving the tibial division would make a more proximal lesion more likely.

findings.title: Dorsiflexion and eversion weakness
findings.reviewed: Weakness affecting both dorsiflexion and eversion supports involvement of muscles supplied by the fibular nerve.
findings.unreviewed: Testing dorsiflexion and eversion together could help identify the affected motor distribution.

findings.title: Preserved inversion and hip abduction
findings.reviewed: Preserved inversion and hip abduction are particularly useful because these movements involve L5 muscles supplied outside the common fibular nerve.
findings.unreviewed: Testing inversion and hip abduction could help distinguish a common fibular lesion from a more proximal L5 nerve root lesion.

findings.title: Sensory distribution
findings.reviewed: Sensory changes involving the lateral shin and dorsal foot, with preserved plantar sensation, support a fibular nerve distribution.
findings.unreviewed: Mapping sensory loss across the dorsal and plantar foot could help localize the deficit more precisely.

supporting_findings.title: Pressure around the fibular head
supporting_findings.reviewed: Prolonged leg crossing provides a plausible mechanism for compression near the fibular head. The motor and sensory examination remains central to localization.

next_steps.title: Confirm localization
next_steps.text: Perform a complete neurological assessment and consider nerve conduction studies and needle EMG to distinguish common fibular neuropathy from L5 radiculopathy or a more proximal peripheral nerve lesion.

next_steps.title: Address contributing factors
next_steps.text: Avoid prolonged compression near the fibular head and assess for potentially reversible causes. Consider targeted imaging around the knee if a structural compressive lesion is suspected.

next_steps.title: Maintain function
next_steps.text: Address gait safety, consider an ankle foot orthosis when appropriate, and initiate rehabilitation directed at maintaining mobility and function.

incorrect.low: It is reasonable to feel uncertain when both root and peripheral nerve lesions can cause foot weakness. Comparing eversion with inversion and mapping dorsal versus plantar sensation provides a practical way to localize the lesion.

cases.title: Clumsy Hands
cases.initial: A 63-year-old accountant reports six months of increasing difficulty with buttons and handwriting. He also mentions some neck discomfort and wonders whether arthritis could be affecting his hands.
aliases: degenerative cervical cord compression causing myelopathy
cervical myelopathy due to degenerative cord compression
questions: Buttons, keys, and handwriting have become noticeably more awkward in both hands.
He has begun using the handrail on stairs and feels less steady when walking on uneven ground.
The hand difficulty and imbalance have gradually worsened rather than appearing in isolated episodes.
He has mild neck stiffness but no prominent shooting pain into a specific arm or finger.
Both hands sometimes feel vaguely numb. He cannot identify a single finger or nerve territory.
There is no urinary retention, incontinence, or new bowel dysfunction.
There has been no fall, accident, or sudden neck injury.
He reports no fever, unexplained weight loss, new visual loss, speech difficulty, or facial weakness.
Gait is mildly broad based, and he struggles to maintain tandem walking without stepping sideways.
Knee reflexes are brisk bilaterally, Hoffmann signs are present, and the right plantar response is extensor.
Rapid finger opening and closing is slow, with mild finger escape on sustained hand extension. Grip strength is only mildly reduced.
There is no clear single dermatome or peripheral nerve pattern. Arm strength is largely preserved except for subtle hand weakness.
imaging: Cervical MRI shows degenerative disc and ligament changes causing marked canal narrowing and cord flattening at C4–C5 and C5–C6. There is a small area of increased T2 signal within the cord at C5.
cases.debrief: Progressive bilateral hand dysfunction together with gait imbalance, brisk reflexes, a pathologic plantar response, and impaired dexterity points to cervical spinal cord dysfunction rather than an isolated hand disorder. Cervical MRI demonstrates concordant cord compression and signal change, supporting degenerative cervical myelopathy.

alternatives.name: Cervical radiculopathy
alternatives.distinction: A nerve root disorder may cause neck pain and focal arm weakness or sensory symptoms. It does not usually account for bilateral long tract findings, an extensor plantar response, and gait impairment.

alternatives.name: Peripheral nerve entrapment
alternatives.distinction: Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome can impair hand sensation and dexterity but does not explain the lower limb reflexes and gait findings.

alternatives.name: Peripheral neuropathy
alternatives.distinction: A generalized neuropathy may affect gait and hand sensation, but the upper motor neuron signs and cord compression favour myelopathy.

findings.title: Upper motor neuron signs
findings.reviewed: Brisk reflexes and a pathologic plantar response point toward central motor pathway involvement and are inconsistent with an isolated distal nerve entrapment.
findings.unreviewed: Checking reflexes and plantar responses could distinguish spinal cord dysfunction from a peripheral hand disorder.

findings.title: Tandem gait
findings.reviewed: Impaired tandem walking adds evidence of a broader neurological syndrome beyond fine motor hand dysfunction.
findings.unreviewed: A focused gait examination could reveal functional consequences of spinal cord involvement.

findings.title: Cervical cord imaging
findings.reviewed: Concordant cervical cord compression with intramedullary signal change supports the clinical localization, though MRI abnormalities still require examination correlation.
findings.unreviewed: Review of available cervical MRI could establish whether there is structural compression explaining the clinical cord signs.

supporting_findings.title: Hand dexterity
supporting_findings.reviewed: Slowed rapid finger movements and finger escape support a cervical cord syndrome in the context of gait and upper motor neuron findings.

next_steps.title: Timely specialist evaluation
next_steps.text: Arrange prompt spine surgery or appropriate specialist assessment because progressive myelopathic symptoms and cord signal change risk further functional decline. Assess severity and trajectory.

next_steps.title: Safety and monitoring
next_steps.text: Review falls risk and new gait, hand, or bladder deterioration. Avoid high force cervical manipulation. New rapidly progressing neurological deficits require urgent reassessment.

next_steps.title: Management planning
next_steps.text: Discuss treatment according to severity and progression. Surgical decompression is frequently indicated in moderate, severe, or progressive disease. Rehabilitation and function support may complement specialist care rather than delaying evaluation.

correct.high: You confidently recognized a cervical cord syndrome. The combination of hand dysfunction, long tract signs, gait change, and matching MRI supports that conclusion.
correct.moderate: You identified the leading diagnosis. Correlating the neurological examination with cord compression on MRI helps distinguish myelopathy from a peripheral hand disorder.
correct.low: You reached the leading diagnosis despite uncertainty. The strongest clues are long tract examination findings together with gait and hand dysfunction.

incorrect.high: Your preferred diagnosis does not fully explain this presentation. Consider whether it accounts for the pathological plantar response, gait imbalance, and cord imaging findings.
incorrect.moderate: Reconsider whether a distal nerve or isolated nerve root lesion can explain both hand symptoms and upper motor neuron signs.
incorrect.low: This presentation spans the hands and legs. Looking for a single neurological localization, then checking the MRI for concordance, can help narrow the differential.

reasoning.correct_high_limited: You confidently recognized a cervical cord syndrome. The combination of hand dysfunction, long tract signs, gait change, and matching MRI supports that conclusion.

missing_feedback.default: In a similar case, combining upper motor neuron examination, gait or hand testing, and cervical MRI would strengthen the clinical localization.

differential_feedback.label: Leading diagnosis

cases.title: Persistent Back Pain
cases.initial: A 27-year-old woman has had lower back and buttock discomfort for approximately 14 months. The symptoms sometimes disrupt her sleep.
aliases: inflammatory spondyloarthritis of the spine and sacroiliac joints
questions: Her back feels stiff for approximately an hour after waking, then gradually loosens up.
Movement and exercise usually improve the discomfort. Prolonged rest tends to make it worse.
Does pain wake her at night?
She sometimes wakes during the second half of the night and feels better after getting up and walking.
Symptoms began gradually. There was no fall, lifting injury, or clear mechanical trigger.
What is the buttock pain like?
The deeper buttock ache sometimes shifts from one side to the other.
Her father has psoriasis. She has never been diagnosed with psoriasis herself.
Any other joint or tendon symptoms?
She has intermittent heel pain near the Achilles insertion, especially on first getting out of bed.
Any red flags or systemic symptoms?
No fever, unexplained weight loss, new bowel or bladder dysfunction, or focal neurological weakness.
Lumbar flexion is mildly restricted. The modified Schober measurement shows reduced excursion for her age.
Several sacroiliac stress maneuvers reproduce her familiar deep buttock discomfort, without a single isolated diagnostic finding.
Leg strength, sensation, reflexes, and straight leg raise are normal. Hip range of motion is preserved.
Mild tenderness is present at the right Achilles insertion without redness or marked swelling.
imaging: Pelvic radiographs show no definite erosions, ankylosis, or established radiographic sacroiliitis.
Sacroiliac MRI demonstrates bilateral subchondral bone marrow edema in a pattern concerning for active sacroiliac inflammation. No clear structural ankylosis is seen.

display_labels.h03: Does pain wake her at night?
display_labels.h05: What is the buttock pain like?
display_labels.h07: Any other joint or tendon symptoms?
display_labels.h08: Any red flags or systemic symptoms?

cases.debrief: An insidious onset before age 45, prolonged morning stiffness, improvement with movement rather than rest, night pain, and alternating buttock discomfort form a characteristic inflammatory back pain pattern. The sacroiliac MRI provides additional supportive evidence of inflammation despite plain radiographs without established structural sacroiliitis. The final diagnosis requires clinical correlation and consideration of MRI mimics.

alternatives.name: Mechanical low back pain
alternatives.distinction: Mechanical pain is common in young adults but is less likely to cause prolonged morning stiffness, relief with movement after rest, and second half of the night pain as a consistent pattern.

alternatives.name: Mechanical sacroiliac pain
alternatives.distinction: The buttock symptoms and positive provocation maneuvers can arise from mechanical SI joint disorders. These tests are not specific for inflammatory disease; the broader symptom pattern and MRI matter.

alternatives.name: Infectious sacroiliitis
alternatives.distinction: Infection warrants consideration when there is acute severe pain, fever, systemic illness, or risk factors. Those features are absent here, and the long fluctuating bilateral course is less suggestive of infection.

findings.title: Prolonged morning stiffness
findings.reviewed: Morning stiffness lasting close to an hour supports an inflammatory rather than purely mechanical pain pattern.
findings.unreviewed: Clarifying morning stiffness duration could help separate inflammatory from mechanical back pain.

findings.title: Improvement with movement
findings.reviewed: Relief with activity and worsening during prolonged rest is a particularly useful feature of inflammatory back pain.
findings.unreviewed: Asking whether exercise or rest changes the symptoms could reveal a characteristic inflammatory pattern.

findings.title: Sacroiliac MRI
findings.reviewed: Sacroiliac marrow edema compatible with active inflammation supports axial spondyloarthritis in this clinical context but is not specific in isolation.
findings.unreviewed: Reviewing available sacroiliac MRI could provide evidence of inflammation not evident on plain radiographs.

supporting_findings.title: Night pain
supporting_findings.reviewed: Waking in the second half of the night with improvement on walking strengthens the inflammatory pattern.

next_steps.title: Confirm the clinical picture
next_steps.text: Assess other spondyloarthritis features, functional impact, inflammatory markers where appropriate, and alternatives for MRI changes. HLA-B27 may contribute to assessment but is neither required nor diagnostic alone.

next_steps.title: Refer and initiate appropriate care
next_steps.text: Arrange rheumatology review. Discuss exercise and physiotherapy, with an NSAID trial when safe and clinically appropriate, alongside assessment of contraindications.

next_steps.title: Plan follow-up
next_steps.text: Review symptoms and function over time. More advanced treatments depend on a confirmed diagnosis and response to first line care and should be directed by rheumatology.

correct.high: You recognized axial spondyloarthritis with high confidence. The inflammatory back pain pattern, supported by the sacroiliac findings, makes this a strong working diagnosis.
correct.moderate: You identified the leading diagnosis. The key is the response to exercise and rest, which is more informative than age or location alone.
correct.low: You reached the leading diagnosis despite uncertainty. Prolonged morning stiffness, night symptoms, and improvement with movement are useful clues to consolidate.

incorrect.high: Your diagnosis differs from the leading explanation. Consider whether it accounts for the inflammatory symptom pattern and the sacroiliac MRI findings together.
incorrect.moderate: A mechanical explanation is tempting in a young adult. Compare its expected relationship with activity and rest against the pattern described here.
incorrect.low: Uncertainty is reasonable because SI joint pain has multiple causes. Clarifying inflammatory back pain features and interpreting imaging in context can narrow the possibilities.

reasoning.correct_high_limited: You recognized axial spondyloarthritis with high confidence. The inflammatory back pain pattern, supported by the sacroiliac findings, makes this a strong working diagnosis.

missing_feedback.default: For similar patients, first establish morning stiffness and the effect of movement, then seek another supporting feature or imaging correlation.

cases.title: Wrist Pain After Injury
cases.initial: A 42-year-old woman returns with persistent right wrist and hand pain ten weeks after a nondisplaced distal radius fracture. Her cast was removed four weeks ago, but using the hand remains painful.
cases.intended: Complex regional pain syndrome following distal radius fracture
cases.debrief: The patient's pain is disproportionate to the expected course of recovery and is accompanied by sensory hypersensitivity, colour and temperature changes, swelling, altered sweating, and restricted movement. The combination of reported symptoms and observed signs is characteristic of complex regional pain syndrome. No single examination finding or imaging result establishes the diagnosis.
questions: She describes persistent burning and aching across the hand and wrist, far more intense than she expected at this stage of recovery.
Even light contact from clothing or bedsheets can cause significant discomfort.
She sometimes notices that her right hand becomes noticeably cooler or more reddish purple than the left.
The right hand frequently appears swollen, and she has noticed differences in sweating between her hands.
She struggles to make a full fist or move her wrist because of pain and stiffness.
Her symptoms became more prominent after cast removal rather than steadily improving with time.
She reports no fever, open wound, drainage, or new injury.
Is the discomfort in one nerve territory?
Symptoms involve much of the hand and wrist rather than following a clear median, ulnar, or radial nerve distribution.
Light touch and gentle movement provoke pronounced pain across the affected hand. The response extends beyond a single peripheral nerve territory.
The right hand is visibly mottled and cooler than the left during examination.
Diffuse swelling is present around the right hand and fingers. Sweating is greater on the affected side.
Wrist and finger movement are restricted by pain and stiffness. The skin is intact, with no drainage or focal spreading erythema. The radial pulse is palpable.
imaging: Repeat wrist radiographs demonstrate interval fracture healing with maintained alignment. No new fracture or displacement is identified. Mild regional osteopenia is noted.

display_labels.h08: Is the discomfort in one nerve territory?

alternatives.name: Postimmobilization pain and stiffness
alternatives.distinction: Pain, weakness, and restricted movement are common after immobilization. However, pronounced allodynia, temperature asymmetry, and altered sweating suggest a broader process than ordinary recovery related stiffness.

alternatives.name: Focal peripheral nerve injury
alternatives.distinction: A median, ulnar, or radial nerve injury may cause neuropathic pain and sensory abnormalities. This patient's findings are regional rather than confined to one nerve territory, and the autonomic features warrant consideration of CRPS.

findings.title: Disproportionate regional pain
findings.reviewed: Persistent regional pain that is substantially greater than expected raises concern for a process beyond uncomplicated fracture recovery.
findings.unreviewed: Clarifying the severity, distribution, and trajectory of pain would help determine whether ordinary postfracture recovery adequately explains the presentation.

findings.title: Allodynia
findings.reviewed: Pain with normally nonpainful touch provides an objective sensory sign supporting CRPS.
findings.unreviewed: Assessing responses to light touch could identify allodynia, an important sensory feature of CRPS.

findings.title: Vasomotor asymmetry
findings.reviewed: Observed differences in colour and temperature provide a vasomotor sign rather than relying on the patient's report alone.
findings.unreviewed: Comparing colour and temperature between limbs could identify objective vasomotor asymmetry.

findings.title: Swelling and sweating
findings.reviewed: Observed swelling and sweating asymmetry contribute another clinical domain supporting the diagnosis.
findings.unreviewed: Assessing swelling and sweating could provide additional objective findings relevant to the CRPS diagnostic criteria.

supporting_findings.title: Fracture healing on radiographs
supporting_findings.reviewed: The radiographs demonstrate ongoing fracture healing without a new structural complication. Mild osteopenia is nonspecific and does not confirm CRPS.

next_steps.title: Reassess and exclude alternatives
next_steps.text: Perform a thorough neurovascular and musculoskeletal assessment, review fracture healing, and investigate concerning findings that could indicate infection, vascular compromise, or another structural complication.

next_steps.title: Begin coordinated rehabilitation
next_steps.text: Where CRPS is the leading diagnosis, early, individualized rehabilitation should focus on restoring movement and function, using appropriately graded activity and desensitization strategies. Avoid unnecessarily prolonged immobilization.

next_steps.title: Manage pain and monitor progress
next_steps.text: Address pain sufficiently to enable functional rehabilitation, consider multidisciplinary pain or rehabilitation support, and follow symptoms, mobility, and daily function over time.

must_not_miss.name: Infection or another acute limb complication
must_not_miss.distinction: Worsening pain and swelling must not automatically be attributed to CRPS. Fever, spreading erythema, drainage, a new focal complication, or signs of vascular compromise would require prompt investigation. The diagnosis of CRPS depends on considering and excluding better explanations.

sources.title: Budapest Criteria
sources.description: A focused reference for the clinical criteria, including the distinction between reported symptoms and observed signs.

diagnosis_notes: The Budapest clinical criteria require disproportionate continuing pain, reported symptoms in at least three of four domains, observed signs in at least two domains, and no other diagnosis that better explains the presentation. The domains are sensory, vasomotor, swelling or sweating, and motor or trophic changes.

Reported symptoms come from the history, such as sensitivity to clothing or episodes of colour change. Observed signs are found on examination, such as pain with light touch, a cooler mottled hand, or visible swelling. These are assessed separately. Fracture healing and the absence of obvious infection do not by themselves exclude every alternative explanation.

correct.high: Well done. You identified the leading diagnosis with high confidence. The regional pain pattern and the combination of reported symptoms and observed signs you explored provide support across several clinical domains.
correct.moderate: Well done. You identified the leading diagnosis with moderate confidence. Separating reported symptoms from observed signs and comparing them across the Budapest domains helps make this impression more convincing.
correct.low: Well done. You reached the leading diagnosis despite uncertainty. Read how sensory, vasomotor, swelling or sweating, and motor findings fit together. No single unusual symptom is sufficient on its own.

incorrect.high: Your final diagnosis differs from the leading explanation here, despite your high confidence. Consider whether it explains the regional hypersensitivity, temperature asymmetry, swelling, and altered sweating together. Healing radiographs alone do not account for that clinical pattern, and competing limb complications still need assessment.
incorrect.moderate: Your final diagnosis differs from the leading explanation here. Compare ordinary recovery related stiffness and focal nerve injury with the regional pattern across the Budapest domains, while considering infection and other limb complications.
incorrect.low: Uncertainty is understandable after a fracture because pain and stiffness can have several causes. Organize the history into reported symptom domains, then look for objective signs in separate examination domains before deciding which explanation fits best.

reasoning.correct_high_limited: Well done. You identified the leading diagnosis with high confidence. The findings below explain why the combination of symptoms and objective signs matters more than an isolated clue.

missing_feedback.default: Before settling on CRPS, establish disproportionate continuing pain and check for symptoms in at least three domains and signs in at least two, while considering better explanations.

cases.title: Hand Weakness
cases.initial: A 59-year-old school administrator reports seven months of right hand weakness and occasional muscle twitching. A previous neck radiograph showed degenerative changes, and she wonders whether the findings could explain her symptoms.
questions: Difficulty opening jars began in the right hand and has gradually spread to the left hand. She now occasionally catches her right foot when walking.
Small involuntary movements occur in the arms and calves, including at rest. She also reports intermittent cramps.
She denies persistent sensory loss, numbness, or tingling.
The weakness is present throughout the day and has gradually worsened. Rest does not restore normal strength.
She has not noticed choking, nasal speech, or a persistent change in voice.
There is no new urinary retention, incontinence, or bowel dysfunction.
No known family history of motor neuron disease or inherited muscle disease.
She has tripped twice but has had no major fall, resting shortness of breath, or difficulty lying flat.
There is atrophy of the right first dorsal interosseous muscle with visible fasciculations in the hands and calves.
Hand intrinsic strength is reduced, particularly on the right. Arm and knee reflexes are brisk, and the right plantar response is extensor despite distal muscle wasting.
Light touch, pinprick, joint position, and vibration are intact. There is no cerebellar dysmetria.
Speech, palate movement, and tongue strength are clinically normal at this visit. There is no visible tongue wasting.
imaging: Cervical MRI shows mild to moderate degenerative changes but no major cord compression or abnormal cervical cord signal to explain the widespread motor findings.

An outside EMG report describes ongoing denervation and chronic neurogenic changes in sampled muscles from cervical and lumbosacral regions, including muscles supplied by different peripheral nerves. Sensory nerve conduction responses are preserved, and no motor conduction block is reported.
cases.debrief: Progressive weakness with muscle wasting and fasciculations suggests lower motor neuron dysfunction, while brisk reflexes and an extensor plantar response indicate upper motor neuron involvement. Preserved sensation, widespread neurogenic EMG abnormalities, and lack of explanatory cervical cord compression make a motor neuron disorder a strong concern. ALS remains a specialist diagnosis requiring appropriate exclusion of other processes, particularly treatable mimics.

alternatives.name: Cervical myelopathy
alternatives.distinction: Cervical cord compression may explain hand dysfunction, brisk reflexes, and gait changes, but the MRI lacks sufficient cord pathology to explain widespread denervation and muscle wasting.

alternatives.name: Multifocal motor neuropathy
alternatives.distinction: This potentially treatable motor neuropathy can produce asymmetric distal weakness and atrophy, often with minimal sensory symptoms. Upper motor neuron signs are not typical, and conduction block would strengthen the alternative diagnosis.

alternatives.name: Myasthenia gravis
alternatives.distinction: A neuromuscular junction disorder may cause weakness but usually produces fatigable symptoms without prominent wasting, fasciculations, or upper motor neuron signs.

findings.title: Muscle wasting and fasciculations
findings.reviewed: Focal wasting with fasciculations supports a lower motor neuron process when paired with objective weakness.
findings.unreviewed: Inspecting muscle bulk and fasciculations could identify lower motor neuron involvement rather than relying on reported twitching alone.

findings.title: Upper motor neuron findings
findings.reviewed: Brisk reflexes and an extensor plantar response despite distal weakness indicate upper motor neuron involvement alongside lower motor neuron signs.
findings.unreviewed: Formal reflex and plantar testing could reveal a second neurological level of involvement and substantially change the differential.

findings.title: Multiregion EMG and NCS
findings.reviewed: Neurogenic abnormalities in multiple body regions with preserved sensory responses and no reported conduction block strengthen concern for motor neuron disease, although they do not independently confirm ALS.
findings.unreviewed: Available EMG and nerve conduction information could help assess the distribution of denervation and evaluate peripheral nerve mimics.

supporting_findings.title: Preserved sensation
supporting_findings.reviewed: The lack of persistent sensory symptoms is compatible with a predominantly motor process but is not diagnostic on its own.

next_steps.title: Prompt specialist review
next_steps.text: Refer urgently to a neuromuscular specialist for confirmation, targeted evaluation for mimics, and discussion of findings in an appropriate clinical setting.

next_steps.title: Complete the assessment
next_steps.text: Review the EMG and nerve conduction study in detail, determine whether further sampling or targeted bloodwork is required, and assess bulbar, respiratory, nutritional, and functional status.

next_steps.title: Coordinate supportive care
next_steps.text: If ALS is confirmed, offer timely multidisciplinary motor neuron disease care, disease modifying therapy discussions according to current eligibility, rehabilitation and assistive equipment, and patient centred planning.

correct.high: You identified the leading concern with high confidence. The combination of progressive motor impairment, upper and lower motor neuron signs, and widespread neurogenic findings strongly supports specialist evaluation for ALS.
correct.moderate: You recognized the leading concern. Correlating the neurological examination with multiregion EMG findings makes motor neuron disease more likely than an isolated cervical lesion.
correct.low: You identified the leading concern despite uncertainty. Seeing upper and lower motor neuron abnormalities together is the key diagnostic turning point in this case.

incorrect.high: Your diagnosis differs from the leading concern. Reconsider whether it can explain both the brisk reflexes and muscle wasting, as well as neurogenic abnormalities outside one root or nerve territory.
incorrect.moderate: This case can resemble a cervical or peripheral nerve problem early on. The broader distribution of motor findings helps distinguish those possibilities.
incorrect.low: Progressive weakness has several possible causes. Use the combination of motor examination, sensory sparing, and electrodiagnostic distribution to guide localization.

reasoning.correct_high_limited: You identified the leading concern with high confidence. The combination of progressive motor impairment, upper and lower motor neuron signs, and widespread neurogenic findings strongly supports specialist evaluation for ALS.

missing_feedback.default: For similar presentations, establishing both upper and lower motor neuron findings and considering the distribution of denervation are central to the assessment.

differential_feedback.label: Relevant alternative
synonyms: multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block

sources.title: Diagnosing ALS: The Gold Coast Criteria and the Role of EMG
sources.description: A concise discussion of clinical diagnostic criteria and the role and limitations of electrodiagnostic testing.

must_not_miss.name: Treatable motor neuron disease mimics
must_not_miss.distinction: Before assigning an ALS diagnosis, investigate alternative structural, immune mediated, metabolic, or neuropathic causes of progressive motor weakness as clinically indicated. A teaching vignette cannot substitute for a complete neuromuscular assessment.

cases.title: Unexplained Buttock Pain
cases.initial: A 41-year-old recreational runner reports six months of right buttock pain with occasional tingling down the back of her thigh. A prior lumbar MRI was described to her as showing a disc bulge, and she wonders whether it explains the pain.
aliases: sciatic nerve entrapment in the deep gluteal space
sciatic nerve compression in the buttock
sciatic nerve entrapment in the deep gluteal region
questions: Sitting, especially during longer drives, brings on a deep buttock ache after about 20 minutes. Standing and walking usually ease it.
Pain is centered deep in the right buttock and sometimes travels down the posterior thigh, rarely beyond the knee.
Any back pain or spinal triggers?
Lower back discomfort is minimal. Coughing, sneezing, and forward bending do not reproduce the characteristic buttock pain.
The pain began gradually after she increased her running distance on hilly routes. There was no fall or acute tear.
Comfortable standing and short walks usually help. Prolonged sitting in a car is much worse than walking.
Tingling is occasional. She has no consistent foot numbness, weakness, or foot drop.
Any bowel or bladder red flags?
No new bowel or bladder problems, saddle sensory change, fever, or unexplained weight loss.
Sitting on a firm chair or applying pressure deep into the affected buttock reproduces her familiar ache.
Flexion, adduction, and internal rotation of the right hip in sitting reproduce the deep buttock pain and familiar posterior thigh symptoms.
Resisted abduction and external rotation reproduce her deep buttock discomfort on the right.
There is focal tenderness deep to the gluteal muscles near the course of the sciatic nerve. The ischial tuberosity is not the principal point of tenderness.
Check lumbar, hip, and nerve findings
Hip joint motion is preserved, straight leg raise does not reproduce her characteristic symptoms, and lower limb strength, sensation, and reflexes are normal at rest.
imaging: Lumbar MRI shows a small central L5–S1 disc bulge without convincing nerve root compression or foraminal narrowing that matches her symptoms.
No dedicated pelvic MRI or imaging of the deep gluteal space has been performed.

display_labels.h03: Any back pain or spinal triggers?
display_labels.h07: Any bowel or bladder red flags?
display_labels.e04: Check lumbar, hip, and nerve findings

cases.debrief: Pain concentrated deep in the buttock, marked intolerance of prolonged sitting, and reproduction of familiar symptoms during two targeted deep gluteal provocative tests support irritation or entrapment of the sciatic nerve outside the spine. A small lumbar disc bulge without concordant nerve root compression does not adequately explain the presentation. This is a clinical working diagnosis, and the tests do not definitively establish the precise structure responsible.

alternatives.name: Lumbar radiculopathy
alternatives.distinction: Radiating posterior leg symptoms can arise from an irritated lumbosacral nerve root. The absence of a convincing spinal trigger, lack of a focal root deficit, and nonconcordant MRI make a spinal source less likely here.

alternatives.name: Proximal hamstring tendinopathy
alternatives.distinction: Pain near the ischial tuberosity may worsen with sitting or running, but hamstring loading and focal tendon origin tenderness would be more characteristic than reproduction of sciatic symptoms during deep gluteal provocation.

alternatives.name: Hip or sacroiliac pathology
alternatives.distinction: Hip joint and SI joint conditions can refer pain to the buttock. A targeted regional examination helps determine whether those structures are more likely to be involved.

findings.title: Sitting intolerance
findings.reviewed: Deep buttock pain provoked by prolonged sitting is a common clinical feature of deep gluteal syndrome, although it can occur in other conditions.
findings.unreviewed: Clarifying which positions provoke symptoms could help distinguish a deep gluteal source from activity related spinal pain.

findings.title: Seated piriformis stretch
findings.reviewed: Reproduction of her familiar deep buttock and thigh symptoms with seated piriformis stretch supports a deep gluteal pain generator in context.
findings.unreviewed: Seated stretch testing could help determine whether tension in the deep gluteal region reproduces the familiar complaint.

findings.title: Active piriformis test
findings.reviewed: Reproduction of symptoms with resisted hip abduction and external rotation adds convergent support for a deep gluteal mechanism.
findings.unreviewed: Active deep gluteal testing could provide additional evidence when interpreted alongside the history and other examination findings.

supporting_findings.title: Nonconcordant lumbar MRI
supporting_findings.reviewed: A minor disc bulge should not automatically be blamed for buttock and leg symptoms when clinical features and anatomical compression do not match.

next_steps.title: Revisit localization
next_steps.text: Complete the lumbar spine, neurological, hip, sacroiliac, and proximal hamstring examinations. Reconsider lumbar or pelvic pathology if new deficits or discordant findings develop.

next_steps.title: Conservative management
next_steps.text: Discuss graded activity, reducing prolonged compressive sitting, and individualized rehabilitation directed at hip and deep gluteal function while monitoring symptom response.

next_steps.title: Further evaluation if persistent
next_steps.text: If pain remains disabling or the diagnosis is uncertain, consider specialist assessment. Targeted pelvic MRI, electrodiagnostic testing, or a carefully selected diagnostic injection may help in particular cases, but none is a universal confirmatory test.

correct.high: You identified the leading working diagnosis confidently. The sitting pattern and concordant deep gluteal provocative findings provide meaningful support for this localization.
correct.moderate: You identified a plausible deep gluteal sciatic nerve disorder. Comparing its physical examination pattern with lumbar and hamstring sources helps strengthen the impression.
correct.low: You arrived at the leading working diagnosis despite uncertainty. The combination of sitting intolerance and reproduction with targeted deep gluteal testing is especially informative.

incorrect.high: Your preferred diagnosis differs from the leading explanation. Ask whether it accounts for both the sitting intolerance and the targeted deep gluteal examination findings.
incorrect.moderate: The old lumbar imaging result is tempting, but structural findings should be weighed against the actual symptom and examination pattern.
incorrect.low: Buttock pain has several plausible causes. Localizing the provoked pain and comparing lumbar, hamstring, and deep gluteal findings can make the next step clearer.

reasoning.correct_high_limited: You identified the leading working diagnosis confidently. The sitting pattern and concordant deep gluteal provocative findings provide meaningful support for this localization.

missing_feedback.default: For similar presentations, combine positional history with both passive and active deep gluteal examination rather than relying on a minor lumbar MRI finding.
